fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, covenant. God says, “I will establish My covenant between Me and you…” A covenant is a binding promise, and this one comes straight from God Almighty. He adds, “…and I will multiply you exceedingly.” Abram is ninety-nine, and that promise does not fit in a cookie box.
That's it. God says, “You will be the father of many nations.” Not one nation. Not two. MANY. Abram is ninety-nine, and God is talking about a family tree with a whole lot of branches.
A royal city sounds fancy, I'll give you that. But God doesn't promise one here. He says, “You will be the father of many nations.” This promise is about people, not buildings.

Yes! God says, “No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.” The new name comes with a reason attached. God doesn't just hand over a new name, He tells Abraham why.

Israel is a name you'll hear later in this story, so I see why it came to mind. But here God says, “…your name will be Abraham…” God later gives the name Israel to Jacob (Genesis 32:28). Jacob is Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), and Isaac is Abraham's son (Genesis 25:19), so that name belongs to Abraham's grandson, down the road.
That's right. God says, “I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.” Nations and kings in the same breath. Abraham is facedown on the ground, and God is still adding to the list.

Prophets are a good guess, and I like the thinking. But God says, “I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.” Kings is the word He picks. I've been known to guess with chocolate chips all over my face, so no shame here, friend.

Moab isn't the land God names here. He says, “…the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan…” Abraham is already living there as a resident. God is promising the place he's staying in right now, so there's not a single box to pack.

A lamb is a good guess, and it sounds like covenant business. But in this talk God says, “Every male among you must be circumcised.” He calls that a sign of the covenant between Him and Abraham (verse 11). No lamb on this list, and I read the fine print twice.

Staying in the household is a sweet guess, but Abraham doesn't ask for that. He says, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” He's asking for God's blessing on his son's life. I think that's a father who wants the very best for his boy.
Isaac is right. God says, “Your wife Sarah will indeed bear you a son, and you are to name him Isaac.” Naming a baby usually takes a whole lot of debating. Here God just says the name.

Joseph is a famous name in this family, but he comes much later. He's Israel's son (Genesis 37:3), and God renames Jacob as Israel (Genesis 32:28). Jacob is Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), so Joseph is Abraham's great-grandson. God's instruction here is, “…you are to name him Isaac.”
Yes. God says Sarah will bear Isaac “…at this time next year.” That's not a vague someday. It's one year out, and Abraham can count toward it.

Next year is when God says Isaac will be born (verse 21), but that's not when Abraham acts. The text says, “On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael…” There's no waiting a year. He does it the same day God finishes speaking.
